lesson.title: Seeing Two Variables at Once: The Scatterplot
lesson.summary: A scatterplot displays pairs of related data as points on a coordinate plane, one variable on each axis, so the overall pattern of the points can reveal a relationship between the two variables.
lesson.body:
You already know how the coordinate plane works, with an x-axis, a y-axis, and points located by ordered pairs, and you know what a data set is, an organized collection of values. A scatterplot combines both ideas. Instead of a single data set, you start with two data sets measured on the same subjects, and you pair them up into ordered pairs, (x, y). Each pair becomes one point plotted on the coordinate plane.

Here is a worked example. Five students report how many hours they studied and the score they earned on a test, giving the paired data set (1, 65), (2, 70), (3, 75), (4, 85), (5, 90), where x is hours studied and y is test score. To plot these, locate (1, 65) one unit right and 65 units up, then (2, 70), then (3, 75), then (4, 85), then (5, 90). It is looking at all five points together as one picture, rather than as five separate, unrelated ordered pairs, that turns this into a scatterplot.

Once the points are plotted, the goal is to look for a pattern. Do the y-values tend to increase as the x-values increase, tend to decrease, or show no consistent pattern at all? How closely do the points cluster near an imaginary trend line running through them, versus how widely do they scatter away from it? Are there any points sitting far apart from the rest of the pattern? In the study-hours example, the five points climb fairly closely together from lower left to upper right: more hours of studying tends to go along with a higher test score.

Describing that upward, downward, or absent trend precisely, and being careful about whether it means one variable is causing the other to change or is simply associated with it, is exactly what the next chapter, correlation, is about.
